extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and graduate students interested in theory change and scientific methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for assessing, comparing, and persuading acceptance of scientific paradigms (how and why one paradigm supplants another). Emphasizes historical, empirical, rhetorical, and community-based factors that influence paradigm change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm change requires crisis from persistent puzzle-solving failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigm-testing occurs only after persistent failure to solve a noteworthy puzzle has given rise to crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science is puzzle-solving and takes the paradigm for granted; only when notable puzzles persistently resist solution does the community face a crisis that can evoke alternate paradigms. Thus, the existence of a recognizably serious crisis/problem-set is a precondition for paradigm competition and possible change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification/testing is competition between rival paradigms, not single-theory tests
rubrics_metrics.description: In the sciences the testing situation never consists simply in the comparison of a single paradigm with nature; testing occurs as part of the competition between two rival paradigms for the allegiance of the scientific community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should be comparative: which of the actual competing theories better accounts for the evidence in the historical situation. Single-instance tests or isolated puzzle attempts do not amount to paradigm testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare theories by their ability to explain existing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilistic and comparative approaches ask us to compare the ability of different theories to explain the evidence at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative fit to available evidence is central to judging theories; however, such comparisons are constrained by the observation-language and concepts available within existing paradigms, limiting claims of absolute verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of probabilistic/neutral verification constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilistic verification approaches demand construction (in imagination) of all tests or alternate theories that might fit the data; such constructions presuppose a neutral observation language that may not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because observation-language and conceptual frameworks are paradigm-dependent, imagined exhaustive comparisons or tests are unrealistic; probabilistic computations thus risk disguising the true, paradigm-relative nature of verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsification is not straightforward as grounds for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure falsification (rejecting a theory because of a negative test) is problematic: no theory ever fits all puzzles perfectly, and ordinary failures-to-fit are not sufficient grounds for rejecting a theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any minor failure were grounds for rejection, all theories would be constantly rejected. Popperian demands for criteria of 'improbability' or 'degree of falsification' encounter difficulties similar to probabilistic verification approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage model: anomaly evokes candidate; later verification is triumph of new paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Anomalous experiences evoke competitors for an existing paradigm; the actual replacement (verification/falsification) is a subsequent process consisting in the triumph of the new paradigm over the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of these distinct stages (anomaly→candidate formation, then paradigm competition/triump) helps explain the historical sequence and the role of comparative arguments in eventual acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incommensurability: differing problem lists, standards, and meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents of competing paradigms often disagree about which problems matter and about non-empirical assumptions; paradigms can change the meaning of terms and the list of legitimate problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because paradigms embody different standards and vocabularies, arguments between them may pass 'through' each other and cannot be resolved purely by shared criteria; this complicates straightforward comparative evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: New paradigms usually incorporate old apparatus but re-relate concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: New paradigms ordinarily borrow vocabulary, instruments, and techniques from the old but employ them in new relationships, producing misunderstandings between competing schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation must attend not only to reused elements but to their reconfigured roles and to how conceptual-web shifts change what counts as explanation or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary persuasive claim: new paradigm can solve crisis-provoking problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The most prevalent and effective claim by proponents of a new paradigm is that it can solve the problems that caused the old paradigm's crisis; 'crucial experiments' that discriminate sharply between paradigms are especially persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legitimate, demonstrable problem-solving in the crisis area can be decisive; historical examples include Copernicus, Newton, Lavoisier, Einstein claiming solutions to central problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative precision and predictive accuracy as strong grounds for conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Display of strikingly better quantitative precision than the older competitor is especially persuasive in converting scientists (e.g., Kepler's tables, Newton's predictive success, Planck/Bohr quantitative fits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a new paradigm yields quantitatively superior predictions that match observations, conversions accelerate; quantitative superiority is often more convincing than qualitative arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel predictions or unexpected phenomena strengthen a paradigm's case
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigms that predict phenomena previously unsuspected under the old paradigm (e.g., phases of Venus, mountains on the moon, Fresnel's white spot) can gain converts rapidly because such predictions are striking and not 'built into' the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprising successful predictions have high persuasive value, especially when they were not contrived to match known data and when they are later observed or experimentally demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic and subjective considerations (neatness, simplicity) matter for early adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that a theory is 'neater', 'more suitable', or 'simpler' can attract early supporters who will develop and exploit the paradigm further; aesthetic appeal can be decisive for a few key converts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although less effective than problem-solving evidence, aesthetic appeal helps secure initial adherents who refine the paradigm into forms that later produce hard technical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance often requires faith in a paradigm's future promise rather than past achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing a new paradigm often depends less on past accomplishments than on faith that it will guide research and solve many unresolved future problems; early adopters act on that faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because new candidates initially solve only a few problems (and imperfectly), willingness to adopt them requires belief they can be developed; prior crisis increases readiness to take that risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion is a social/community process: development, texts, instruments multiply support
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporters who are competent will improve the candidate paradigm, explore its possibilities, and demonstrate what membership in its community looks like; as experiments, instruments, publications based on it multiply, more converts follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of a paradigm should include its capacity to be developed by a committed community—generation of research programs, instruments, educational texts, and professional networks is crucial for eventual triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single decisive argument; distributional shift of allegiances matters
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single argument that can or should persuade all scientists; rather, acceptance occurs via an increasing shift in the distribution of professional allegiances as multiple arguments cumulatively persuade different subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should not expect a single logical proof; instead, consider the plurality of persuasive strategies and the aggregate movement within the community over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual nature of verification (natural-selection analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification operates like natural selection: it picks out the most viable among the actual alternatives in a particular historical situation; whether the choice is the best possible in some other context is not a useful question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation is historically bounded—what counts as the 'best' explanation depends on the available alternatives, problems deemed relevant, and the conceptual resources of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication limits across paradigms limit purely logical persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Because competing paradigms involve different conceptual webs, conversion cannot be forced by logic and neutral experience; full communication requires undergoing the conceptual transformation characteristic of the other paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasion strategies must account for partial communication: conceptual reorientation (sometimes dramatic) is necessary before opponents can fully see what proponents see.
